_failedBecause: The user rejected the whole round: 'negative, i need humanoid mech, this current round is useless to me, dispose it.' The style lock WORKED - all five machines shared one palette, one camera and one light - but every subject was non-humanoid (quadruped, hexapod, tripod). The technique is worth keeping; the subject form was wrong. Recipe retained as a failure record.
_comment: Round 05 - FIVE war mechs, five different archetypes, ONE locked art style. The lesson from round 04: the set was rejected for style drift ('one can look like a mech from a fiction movie and the other is mech from another movie'). The cause was that each concept carried its OWN palette and wear sentence, so the model faithfully drew five machines from five different films. The fix here: the livery, materials, construction vocabulary, camera and lighting live ONLY in the shared styleSuffix. Every concept describes ONLY archetype, pose and weapon - never colour, never material, never finish. Five classes (quadruped hunter, hexapod artillery, tripod sentinel, heavy ram, long crawler) from one production line. Studio backdrop unchanged. All SUBJECT boxes are wider than they are tall, because round 04's four tall boxes produced four upright humanoid rejects and its only wide box produced the only keeper.
_styleLock: If a future round drifts back into five different films, check first: does any concept sentence mention a colour, a material or a finish? It must not. Colour and finish live in styleSuffix and nowhere else.
promptPrefix: A full-body concept-art portrait of an armoured war machine, a legged combat robot with a wide horizontal chassis, a low angular sensor head and heavy weapons integrated into the frame,
styleSuffix: . Every machine in this series is built to one identical design standard: matte gunmetal armour plates in stacked segments, a matte charcoal underframe with charcoal legs and weapon housings, one narrow signal-amber accent strip running along the upper flank, and pale bone-white ceramic panels on the sensor housing and the raised upper plates of the hull. The same family of low angular sensor heads, the same chunky hydraulic leg joints and the same broad clawed feet on every machine, so the set reads as one production line built by one manufacturer. Clean unmarked plate surfaces, hard-edged faceted forms, no rivets and no bare steel. Every machine shows the same light even field wear: a uniform chalky grey dust film on the upward-facing surfaces and faint scuffs on the leading edges. Shot identically on every machine: a three-quarter front view from the left, camera at the height of the machine's hull, a 50mm lens, the whole machine in frame with clear air around it. Standing on a seamless neutral silver-grey studio backdrop with a soft contact shadow under its body. The backdrop is plain and empty: no landscape, no sky, no horizon, no ground scenery, no buildings, no props, no weapons on the ground, no rubble. Nothing else in the frame except the machine and its shadow. Military concept art in a painterly semi-realistic real-robot mecha illustration style, smooth airbrushed gradients, soft volumetric haze, gentle film grain, studio key light high above and slightly to the left, falling on the machine only, cool soft fill on the camera-facing side, a bright thin edge highlight running down the left side of the machine, flat even overhead ambient lighting on the floor, the floor a matte plane of one uniform neutral grey with no horizontal gradient across it, all the way to every edge of the frame, with no directional falloff, no pool of light, no bright corner, no dark corner and no reflection. Huge readable silhouette, crisp negative space between the limbs, fine mechanical detail, deep contact shadows. No text, no lettering, no watermark, no scenery, no extra limbs, no duplicated parts.
